commitResults.messageBody:
Several methods rely on assumptions that are never verified at
runtime, e.g. that a value already validated by a caller stays
valid, or that a helper method never returns null. These
assumptions are easy to break silently during future changes,
since nothing currently catches a violated invariant until it
surfaces later as a confusing, unrelated bug.

Let's add `assert` statements at the points where these
assumptions are made, so a broken invariant fails loudly and
close to its source instead.

Assertions are added for:
* postconditions on Task#markAsDone() and #unmarkAsDone(), that
  isDone reflects the requested state after the method returns
* the shape of split() results in DeadlineTask#create() and
  EventTask#create(), guaranteed by the contains()/indexOf()
  checks immediately preceding them
* Command#parse() never returning null
* Parser#handleInput()'s parameters never being null, and its
  return value never being null in Penny#respond()
* MainWindow#handleUserInput() never running before setPenny()
  has injected a Penny instance

Assertions are deliberately not used for anything derived from
user input (e.g. command arguments, indices typed by the user),
since those are real, expected failure paths that must still be
reported via PennyException regardless of whether assertions
are enabled.

Since the JVM disables assertions by default unless started
with -ea, also enable them on the run, runGui, and runCli
Gradle tasks so they actually take effect outside of test
(which Gradle already enables assertions for by default).

The LIST, DUE, and FIND cases in Parser#handleInput() each loop
over the task list, filter it by a different condition (no
filter, due-date match, keyword match), and format the matches
as a "1. task" numbered list joined by newlines. The three loops
are identical apart from the filter condition, which is exactly
the kind of duplication the "Minimize Code Duplication"
guideline in the course's code quality guide warns against.

Let's extract that shared shape into a private
formatNumbered(TaskList, Predicate<Task>) helper, and have each
case supply only its own filter as a lambda.

A single parameterised helper is preferable to three separate
near-identical methods (e.g. formatList/formatDue/formatFind),
since the only thing that actually varies between the three call
sites is the filter condition, not the looping or formatting
logic around it.

No behavioural change: verified against the existing ParserTest
suite, and manually re-checked list/find/due via runCli.

commitResults.messageTitle: Parser: extract one handler method per command
commitResults.messageBody:
handleInput() held an 11-way switch where every case mixed
argument validation, task-list mutation, and result-building at
different levels of detail in one ~140-line method. That makes
it hard to see any single command's logic at a glance, and it is
exactly what the code quality guide's "Avoid Long Methods" and
"SLAP" (single level of abstraction per method) guidelines flag.

Let's extract each case's body into its own private
handleBye/handleList/handleDue/... method, so handleInput()
becomes a thin dispatcher that just parses the command and
delegates, and each handler reads as one self-contained unit at
a single level of abstraction.

No behavioural change: verified against the existing ParserTest
suite, and manually re-checked todo/mark/unmark/delete/list via
runCli.

Checkstyle already fails on this branch independently of this
change (e.g. import order and a missing Javadoc comment on
isInteger(), both present before this commit too, confirmed via
git stash) - that is pre-existing and out of scope here, left
for a dedicated checkstyle pass.

commitResults.messageTitle: DeadlineTask, EventTask: name the delimiter tokens
commitResults.messageBody:
DeadlineTask#create() checks for and splits on the literal
"/by" in two separate places, and EventTask#create() does the
same with "/from" and "/to" - each token spelled out twice with
nothing tying the two occurrences together. EventTask also adds
arguments.substring(fromIndex + 5), where 5 is silently
"/from".length(): a magic number a reader has to reverse-engineer
to understand. These are exactly what the code quality guide's
"Avoid Magic Numbers" guideline warns about, generalised to
string literals doing the same job as a numeric constant here.

Let's give each delimiter its own private static final constant
(BY_KEYWORD, FROM_KEYWORD, TO_KEYWORD) and use it everywhere the
literal previously appeared, including the offset arithmetic in
EventTask, which becomes fromIndex + FROM_KEYWORD.length().

This also means a future change to a delimiter (unlikely, but
possible) only has to happen in one place per class instead of
staying in sync across two call sites by hand.

No behavioural change: verified against the existing ParserTest
suite, and manually re-checked deadline/event creation via
runCli.

unmarkAsDone()'s own Javadoc says it throws when "the task is
already marked as undone", but the code actually throws "Task is
already marked as done" - the literal opposite, and a copy-paste
leftover from markAsDone()'s identical guard. A user unmarking an
already-undone task sees a message claiming it is done, which is
exactly the kind of misleading text the code quality guide's
"Avoid Misleading Names" guideline warns against, applied here to
an error message rather than an identifier.

Let's change the message to "Task is already marked as undone",
matching what the method's own Javadoc already documents.

No test asserted on the old string, so nothing else needed to
change. Verified via the existing ParserTest/TaskListTest suite,
and manually via runCli: unmarking a never-marked task now
reports the corrected message.

commitResults.messageTitle: DateTime: hoist parse() formatters to constants
commitResults.messageBody:
format() already stores its two DateTimeFormatters as private
static final fields at the top of the class, but parse() builds
its own two formatters as fresh local objects on every single
call instead of following the same pattern. That is inconsistent
within one small class, and it means every parse() call pays for
allocating two DateTimeFormatter objects it does not need to -
DateTimeFormatter is immutable and safe to share, which is
exactly why format()'s formatters are already constants.

Let's move parse()'s two formatters up next to the existing
FORMAT_DATE_TIME/FORMAT_DATE constants, named PARSE_DATE_TIME
and PARSE_DATE to mirror that naming, and have parse() reference
them instead of constructing its own copies.

No behavioural change: verified against the existing ParserTest
suite, and manually re-checked both date formats, the
midnight-default path, and the invalid-format error path via
runCli.

commitResults.messageTitle: ToDoTask: rename constructor param to description
commitResults.messageBody:
DeadlineTask and EventTask's protected constructors both name
their description parameter "description", but ToDoTask's
equivalent constructor calls the same thing "arguments" instead
- the same role, named differently for no reason across three
sibling classes. That is exactly the kind of inconsistency the
code quality guide's "Name Well: keep related items similarly
named" guideline calls out, and it makes ToDoTask read like it
does something different from its siblings when it does not.

Let's rename that parameter to "description", matching
DeadlineTask and EventTask. create()'s own "arguments" parameter
is left as-is, since at that point it genuinely is the raw,
unparsed argument string, same as in DeadlineTask#create() and
EventTask#create().

No behavioural change: verified against the existing ParserTest
suite, and manually re-checked todo creation (including
description trimming) via runCli.

flip()'s local variable is named "tmp", which says nothing about
what it actually holds - the dialog box's children in reversed
order, used to put the avatar on the left instead of the right
for Penny's replies. A vague name like "tmp" forces a reader to
trace the two lines that follow it just to find out what it is,
which is what the code quality guide's naming guidance ("Use
Names to Explain": choose descriptive names that clarify purpose
and intent) is there to prevent.

Let's rename it to "reversedChildren", so the variable states
its own purpose and the two lines using it need no extra
tracing to understand.

No behavioural change: same object, same Collections.reverse()/
setAll() calls, just a clearer name. Verified via compilation
and the existing test suite; DialogBox itself has no JUnit
coverage since it is JavaFX UI code, so this was not separately
exercised through the running GUI.

commitResults.messageTitle: Parser: use Streams for LIST, DUE, and FIND
commitResults.messageBody:
The LIST, DUE, and FIND cases each build their numbered result
with an explicit for-loop: initialise an ArrayList<String>,
optionally check a predicate, append a "1. task" string, then
join with String.join() outside the loop. That is a textbook
filter-map-join shape, which java.util.stream exists to express
directly instead of via mutable accumulator state.

Let's replace each loop with an IntStream.range(0, tasks.size())
pipeline: filter() for DUE/FIND's predicate (LIST needs none),
mapToObj() to format the numbered line, and
Collectors.joining("\n") in place of the explicit ArrayList and
String.join() call. IntStream.range() (rather than tasks.stream()
directly, which TaskList does not currently expose anyway) is
used specifically because the numbering must stay relative to
each task's original position, not its position after filtering
- indexing by i preserves that, while filtering the tasks first
would not.

Penny#Penny() and #main()'s loops are deliberately left as
regular loops: the constructor's loop has three side effects per
iteration and must catch a checked PennyException, and main()'s
while(true) is an interactive stdin read loop, not a bounded
collection - neither is a good fit for Streams.

No behavioural change: verified against the existing ParserTest
suite, and manually re-checked list/find/due (including both
their empty-result exception paths) via runCli.
Add assertions to document code invariants
Parser: use Streams for LIST, DUE, and FIND

The Checkstyle setup on branch-A-Checkstyle was never actually
satisfied by the rest of the codebase - it just sat there
unenforced until the new GitHub Actions workflow ran the full
./gradlew check task and turned every push red. 22 errors and 2
warnings were spread across 10 files, in main and (previously
unchecked) test sources alike: missing whitespace before '{' on
one-line class/method declarations, three files missing a
trailing newline, a doubled space before a comment, two
constant-styled instance fields that aren't actually constants,
a method with no Javadoc, and import statements in both test
classes that were not grouped/sorted per the project's
CustomImportOrder rule (static imports first, then org.*
imports, both alphabetical).

Let's fix each violation directly, with no behavioural changes:
whitespace/newline/import-order fixes are purely cosmetic, the
IMAGE_USER/IMAGE_PENNY -> imageUser/imagePenny rename in
MainWindow only touches identifiers (all call sites updated),
and isInteger() gets a Javadoc comment describing what was
already implemented.

Verified with ./gradlew check: all 17 tests pass, checkstyleMain
and checkstyleTest both report zero violations. Also manually
re-checked the CLI (todo/mark/unmark) and confirmed the GUI
still launches cleanly after the MainWindow field rename.

commitResults.messageTitle: Reject tasks whose description is already on the list
commitResults.messageBody:
Nothing currently stops the same task from being added twice.
Two "todo read book" entries, or a "deadline submit report /by
X" alongside an unrelated "event submit report /from Y /to Z",
both silently succeed today even though they describe the same
piece of work - the date/type differs but the task itself does
not, so the list ends up tracking duplicates the user has no
way to tell apart at a glance.

Let's reject a new task whenever its description already
belongs to an existing task, regardless of that task's type or
any dates involved. TaskList gains hasDescription(String), a
simple query consistent with its existing isEmpty()/size()-style
API (Task itself gains a getDescription() accessor to support
it, since none existed). Parser gains a private ensureUnique()
helper called from handleTodo/handleDeadline/handleEvent, right
after each one constructs its Task but before adding it, so all
three commands enforce the same rule through one shared check
instead of three copies of it.

Verified with ./gradlew check: all tests pass (four new ones
covering hasDescription() directly and handleInput()'s rejection,
including the cross-type/cross-date case), checkstyleMain and
checkstyleTest both stay clean. Also manually re-checked via
runCli that a duplicate is rejected across todo/deadline/event
while a genuinely different description is still added normally.
